newsitem.title: ITALY: Belgium, Sweden take steps in Italy cheese scare.
newsitem.headline: Belgium, Sweden take steps in Italy cheese scare.

text.p: Italian health inspectors said on Monday they had pulled some 100,000 tubs of mascarpone cheese from stores over a botulism scare linked to the death of a teenage boy.

Belgium said it too would pull all mascarpone -- a soft, sweet cheese used in desserts -- under the Giglio, Parmalat and Sol di Valle brand names, while Sweden warned consumers not to eat those brands until more was known about the scare.
A spokesman for Sweden's National Food Administration said Sweden's one importer of mascarpone had suspended imports as of Monday "of his own accord until further notice."
The scare began when Nicola Sagiomo, 15, died on Saturday after being admitted to hospital in Naples, southern Italy, with severe stomach cramps.
His younger brother and a friend were also seriously ill in hospital after the three boys had eaten home-made tiramisu, a popular sponge dessert prepared with mascarpone.
They are among at least seven certified cases of botulism that have arisen in the Naples area, the Calabria region on the toe of Italy and the central town of Siena.
All have been linked to a batch of mascarpone with a sell-by date of October 3 produced by one manufacturer in the northern town of Reggio Emilia.

Prosecutors in Naples opened an investigation into the source of the botulism, while health officials from the region including Naples told consumers the situation was under control and there was no need for consumer alarm.
Botulism is a severe form of poisoning from foods that contain a toxin which can affect the central nervous system. In fatal cases, death is often caused by heart and lung failure.
The bacterium is most typically found in improperly preserved canned raw meat.
Giglio SpA said in a statement that "the search for responsibility needs much prudence.

"The formation of botulism toxins in mascarpone is very improbable," the Giglio statement said. "Historically, there are no known cases of botulism contamination in all dairy products which are biologically hostile to the development of botulism toxins."
Health Ministry under-secretary Bruno Viserta said the ministry was awaiting the results of laboratory analysis of the product to assess the extent of the contamination.
He told La Repubblica newspaper that "tests have confirmed the diagnosis of doctors" that the botulism was in the cheese.
